clue.text: The easy way to Beacons field, perhaps

definitions.text: The easy way to Beacons field, perhaps

parts.words: The easy way to Beacons field, perhaps
parts.note: the primrose was Disraeli's favourite flower, and Disraeli became Earl of Beaconsfield, so his route is lined with them; the phrase also means the path of easy pleasure

explanation.surface: Directions for the simplest route to Beaconsfield, a town in Buckinghamshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Disraeli was made Earl of Beaconsfield, and Primrose Day honoured him because the primrose was said to be his favourite flower. The OCR split the place name Beaconsfield in two.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from Hamlet, names a life of pleasure and indulgence, the easy road to ruin.

clue.text: " This earth, this — this England" (Rich. II)

parts.note: John of Gaunt's speech in Shakespeare's Richard II runs: this blessed plot, this earth, this kingdom, this England

explanation.surface: A quotation from John of Gaunt's famous patriotic speech, with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means a kingdom, the sense the speech needs between earth and England.

clue.text: Simon copes (anag:)

indicators.note: the clue spells out that its words are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man named Simon managing, with a bare instruction attached.
explanation.walkthrough: An early-style clue with no definition: the letters of SIMON COPES rearranged give the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Meconopsis is the genus of Himalayan blue poppies and Welsh poppies.

clue.text: Get on with the source of a great amen

definitions.text: Get on with the source of a great amen

parts.words: the source of a great amen
parts.note: in the song The Lost Chord the organ sounds like the sound of a great Amen
taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to carry on alongside the church music.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lost Chord is a Victorian song in which an organ chord rings out like a great Amen. The clue has no separate definition; the whole is wordplay for Aristotle's term.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle's logical treatises are collectively called by this name, meaning instrument of thought.

clue.text: Turn the axe to the pit

definitions.text: Turn the axe to the pit

indicators.note: turn means rearrange, so the word axe is shuffled

parts.note: a mine is a pit, as in a coal pit

explanation.surface: An order to take the axe down the coal pit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' rearranges the letters of axe. There is no separate definition: inspecting a pit is the sense the whole clue suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To inspect or scrutinise closely, as a mining inspector does a pit.

clue.text: An afterthought signed "E"

parts.note: an gives the letter A
a PS, or postscript, is an afterthought at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A postscript to a letter, signed with the initial E.
explanation.walkthrough: An apse is the rounded end of a church, built on after the main body, like a postscript.
explanation.definitionFit: The semicircular recess at the east end of a church is added to the end of the building.

clue.text: Sligo ? Ah, no : (anag.)

indicators.note: the clue openly tells the solver to rearrange the preceding words

explanation.surface: Someone refusing a trip to Sligo, a county in the west of Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: An early-style clue with no definition: SLIGO AH NO rearranged gives rowdy youths.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruffians or louts who cause disorder, often young troublemakers.

clue.text: You must have seen me in one of these caps, my dear Watson

definitions.text: You must have seen me in one of these caps, my dear Watson

parts.words: You must have seen me in one of these caps, my dear Watson
parts.note: Sherlock Holmes is pictured in the double-peaked hunting cap, and addresses Watson so

explanation.surface: Sherlock Holmes telling Dr Watson about his headgear.
explanation.definitionFit: These double-peaked tweed hunting caps, worn for deer hunting, are Holmes's trademark.

clue.text: The cash is less than the country

indicators.note: the money is the country's name made smaller, so a letter is dropped from it

parts.note: France is the country whose old currency this was

explanation.surface: A grumble that a nation's money is worth less than the nation itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less than' takes the final E off FRANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: The franc was the French unit of currency before the euro, so it is that nation's money.

clue.text: The cry proclaimed for clearing the course

definitions.text: The cry proclaimed for clearing the course

parts.note: fore is the golfer's warning shout to people ahead on the course
ordained means decreed or proclaimed

explanation.surface: A shout given out to clear golfers off the course ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: The words 'for clearing the course' explain FORE, the golfer's warning; the answer means decided in advance.
explanation.definitionFit: Predestined: settled beforehand by decree, as fate is said to be.

clue.text: Happy rock of statesmanship

parts.note: glad means happy
a stone is a piece of rock

explanation.surface: A cheerful pillar of the political world.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes W. E. Gladstone, the Victorian Liberal prime minister, a rock of statesmanship.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladstone was four times British prime minister, a byword for Victorian political leadership.

clue.text: A thoughtful group, given to chewing

definitions.text: A thoughtful group, given to chewing

parts.words: A thoughtful group, given to chewing
parts.note: to ruminate is both to ponder and to chew the cud, so cud-chewing animals sound like deep thinkers

explanation.surface: A pensive gathering of people who like to chew things over.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the zoological order of cud-chewing mammals such as cattle, sheep and deer.

clue.text: It enables the landsman to go to sea

definitions.text: It enables the landsman to go to sea

parts.words: It enables the landsman to go to sea
parts.note: a landlubber can walk out over the water on this structure without ever boarding a ship

explanation.surface: Something that lets a land-dweller set out on the ocean, like a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaside jetty projects out over the water, so walkers stroll above the sea.

clue.text: Plant that might be mistaken for a baby-carriage

definitions.text: Plant that might be mistaken for a baby-carriage

parts.words: Plant that might be mistaken for a baby-carriage
parts.note: storks are said to bring babies, carried in their beaks, so this wild geranium's name sounds like a baby transport

explanation.surface: A plant so shaped it looks like a pram.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a wild geranium, Erodium, whose long beaked seed pods resemble a bird's beak.

clue.text: Sacks the piper ?

parts.note: to sack someone is to oust or throw them out, so outs means sacks
the god Pan is famous for playing the pan pipes

explanation.surface: A question whether the musician has been fired.
explanation.walkthrough: To outspan, a South African term, is to unharness oxen from a wagon: letting the team go, as if sacking them.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to unyoke draught animals and release them from work, a kind of dismissal.

clue.text: French husband encumbered with chores

indicators.note: the husband is loaded down by the chores, so they surround him

parts.note: tasks are chores
mari is French for husband

explanation.surface: A Frenchman weighed down by housework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'encumbered with' puts the husband inside the chores. The clue never names the shrub; early Times clues could be wordplay alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamarisks are feathery-leaved shrubs that grow well by the sea.

clue.text: Take out a quotation

definitions.meaning: to remove or draw something out
a passage taken from a book or speech

explanation.surface: Remove a quotation from a text.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means pull out; as a noun it is a passage copied from a longer text.

clue.text: Don't say " Look alive !" to them

definitions.text: Don't say " Look alive !" to them

parts.words: Don't say " Look alive !" to them
parts.note: shop-window mannequins and tailor's figures cannot liven up, being lifeless

explanation.surface: A sergeant's advice not to bark orders at a certain group.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressmakers' figures and mannequins are lifelike models with no life in them.

clue.text: Set about a plant for drink

indicators.note: set goes around the plant, enclosing it

parts.note: a herb is a plant

explanation.surface: Setting up a plant to make a beverage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' looks like a verb but is the outer piece; 'about' puts the plant inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherbet is a sweet fruit-flavoured cooling beverage of Eastern origin.

clue.text: It is put away rather than up just now

definitions.text: It is put away rather than up just now

parts.words: It is put away rather than up just now
parts.note: a sunshade is put up in summer weather, but out of season it is stored away

explanation.surface: Something being stored rather than raised at the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle appeared out of the sunny season, when sunshades are stowed.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a sunshade, an umbrella against the sun, opened only in bright weather.

clue.text: The Roman seems to have pleaded guilty

definitions.text: The Roman seems to have pleaded guilty

parts.words: The Roman seems to have pleaded guilty
parts.note: a Latin speaker confessing would say the Latin for I have sinned

explanation.surface: An ancient Roman apparently confessing in court.
explanation.walkthrough: General Napier reputedly reported taking Sindh with this one Latin word, punning on I have sinned.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word means I have sinned, a confession of fault.

clue.text: Four join the miniature railway

parts.note: IV is four in Roman numerals
RY is the shortened form of railway, a miniature of the word

explanation.surface: Four people climbing aboard a small-gauge railway.
explanation.walkthrough: Early Times clues could be wordplay alone: this one names no place, just builds Ivry, the town near Paris and scene of Henri IV's victory in 1590.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivry is the French battlefield of Macaulay's poem, a town south-east of Paris.

clue.text: Noisy cymbalically speaking

parts.note: cymbalically plays on symbolically; in the world of cymbals and drums, loud means struck

explanation.surface: A remark about something being loud in a figurative way.
explanation.definitionFit: Percussion instruments sound by being struck, so drum-and-cymbal noise is of that striking kind.

clue.text: Discovered in presence of mind I admit-

definitions.text: Discovered in presence of mind I admit-

indicators.note: discovered means uncovered, so the word is found lying within these letters

explanation.surface: Someone owning up to showing quick thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered in' finds the letters in mIND I Admit; India was the land Columbus set out to discover.
explanation.definitionFit: The subcontinent was the goal of explorers like Columbus and da Gama.

clue.text: A vote for the French

parts.note: X is the cross marked on a ballot paper
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A ballot cast in favour of France.
explanation.walkthrough: An early-style clue that builds the word with no definition: the shaft a wheel turns on.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the rod or spindle on which a wheel revolves.

clue.text: To be given a kiss,' and where

parts.note: esse is Latin for to be
X is the cross for a kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Someone asking to be kissed, and asking where.
explanation.walkthrough: ESSEX is an English county east of London, so it answers 'where'.
explanation.definitionFit: A county is a place, so the name answers the question of location.

clue.text: The feathered serpent

parts.note: the word names both a long feathery scarf and a constricting snake

explanation.surface: Quetzalcoatl, the plumed snake god of the Aztecs.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a constrictor snake and a long fluffy stole of feathers, so a serpent of plumes.

clue.text: River on the way to work

indicators.note: only part of the word for work is reached, the journey stopping short before its end

parts.note: industry means hard work

explanation.surface: A river passed while commuting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the way to' stops short of TRY in INDUSTRY.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the great river of Pakistan, flowing from Tibet to the Arabian Sea.

clue.text: Pear plant?

parts.note: the Williams is a well-known variety of pear, and a sweet one, so a sweet pear could be this garden flower

explanation.surface: A query about a fruit tree.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a garden pink, Dianthus barbatus, a cottage flower; Williams is also a pear variety.
